extracted.intended_audience: mathematics researchers and students (graduate and above) working on proofs and research problems
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for mathematicians on pausing to view the big picture when formulating and proving lemmas, claims, and theorems; includes questions to refine statements so work is more efficient and useful. Applicable at scales from small claims to major research goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pause and recall the purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: It is really easy to get bogged down in the details of some work and not recall the purpose of what one is actually doing; thus it is good to pause every now and then and recall why one is pursuing a particular goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly step back from technical details to remind yourself of the overarching goal; this prevents wasting effort on unimportant technicalities and keeps effort aligned to outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask how the lemma will be used
rubrics_metrics.description: If the lemma were proven, how would it be used?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before proving a lemma, explicitly identify its intended use(s); this informs which parts of the statement are essential and which can be relaxed or omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the most important features
rubrics_metrics.description: What features of the lemma are most important for you?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pinpoint which conclusions, bounds, or structural properties are actually needed downstream so you can focus effort on proving those rather than unnecessary extras.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer weaker (sufficient) statements when possible
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether a weaker/less precise statement would already serve the intended application; proving a weaker but sufficient result can save time and simplify arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for simpler formulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there a simpler formulation of the lemma?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek rephrasings or alternative forms of the statement that are clearer or easier to prove while still serving the intended purpose; simpler statements often expose better proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question hard hypotheses — consider omitting them
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it worth trying to omit a hypothesis of the lemma, if that hypothesis seems hard to obtain in practice?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a hypothesis is difficult to verify in examples, ask whether the application truly needs it; removing or weakening such hypotheses can make the lemma more usable and the proof effort more worthwhile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply this 'think ahead' principle at multiple scales
rubrics_metrics.description: The same type of principle applies at scales smaller than lemmas (e.g. when trying to prove a small claim, or to perform a lengthy computation) and at scales larger than lemmas (e.g. when trying to prove a theorem, solve a research problem, or pursue a research goal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the listed questions and the habit of stepping back both for tiny technical steps and for long-term research planning to ensure efficiency and alignment of effort across all stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reformulate statements to an optimal form before proving
rubrics_metrics.description: These questions can help you reformulate your lemma to its optimal form before sinking too much time into trying to prove it, thus enabling you to use your research time more efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize spending time shaping the statement (strength, hypotheses, formulation) so the subsequent proof work targets an optimally useful and provable claim.
